abstract: "Political scientists increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to annotate text. Model, prompt, and inference choices can alter results and create researcher degrees of freedom. We ask how researchers can choose a defensible annotation pipeline without testing every configuration. We vary model choice and prompting condition across political science annotation tasks, using open-weight LLMs. Separate within-family comparisons examine model size. We hold hardware constant and freeze each task\u2019s codebook. We then simulate selection strategies using human-coded validation data and evaluate selected pipelines on held-out texts. After the task itself, task\u2013model interaction explains the largest share of performance variation. Overall model rankings are poor indicators of performance for a particular codebook. Prompting has little average effect but can substantially change performance for individual model\u2013task combinations. Validation can screen out weak pipelines but often cannot identify a unique best one. Testing shortlisted models zero-shot yields nearly the same held-out performance as exhaustive search, with much less energy. We recommend screen-then-expand: stop when the study\u2019s pre-set performance threshold is met, then select the most efficient configuration within a pre-set margin of the best validation score. We also propose annotation-specific reporting standards. Accompanying open-source tools support codebook development and pipeline benchmarking."
